concepts.plain: The GPU's own fast memory, fixed in size. **Weights**, **scratch space** and the **KV cache** share it.
concepts.analogy: A kitchen counter of fixed size: the recipe book takes most of it, a prep area stays clear, order notes fill the rest.
concepts.why: The KV cache gets whatever weights and scratch leave, so free memory decides how many users you can serve.

concepts.plain: The model's learned numbers, on the GPU before it can answer: about 16 GB for an 8B model at 2 bytes per parameter.
concepts.analogy: The recipe book: big, never edited, on the counter before cooking starts.
concepts.why: Loading them sits inside the longest phase of artifact 1's cold start; a weight cache cut that phase by about 15 s.

concepts.plain: While generating, the model keeps the **keys (K) and values (V)** of every token so far instead of recomputing them. Q is not cached.
concepts.analogy: Each open order's notes, one line per token: long orders take more counter, so fewer fit.
concepts.why: Each request holds cache in proportion to its length, so the cache divides into a number of concurrent requests; past that, new ones wait.

concepts.plain: The serving engine here. At startup it loads the weights, runs the model once to see what memory is left, and gives that to the KV cache.
concepts.analogy: Before opening, cook the biggest order once to see how much counter cooking needs; order notes get the rest.
concepts.why: That **memory-profiling** run is in every cold start, and it sets the cache size.

concepts.plain: One copy of the model serving many users' requests at once. A fresh replica takes work as soon as it is ready.
concepts.analogy: One kitchen cooking many orders at once: more dishes per hour, each a little slower.
concepts.why: In artifact 2, as requests in flight rose to 128, one replica's throughput rose and bent while latency rose gently.

concepts.plain: The wait from a request being queued to a brand-new replica's first token.
concepts.analogy: Opening a kitchen from empty when a crowd arrives: get a building, bring in the recipe book, prep, then cook.
concepts.why: It is artifact 1's subject: a median 81.12 s with nothing cached, mostly launching and loading the model, then compiling.

concepts.plain: GPU replicas added when traffic needs them and removed after. Before your code runs, the platform queues the request, finds a machine and starts a container.
concepts.analogy: Renting kitchens as crowds come and go, paying even while one is still opening (artifact 2 counts every replica-second).
concepts.why: Nothing of yours runs during the platform's part, so it is found by subtraction: total time minus the replica's own time.

concepts.plain: Startup steps that pay now to be faster later. **torch.compile** makes faster GPU code and caches it on disk; **CUDA graph capture** records GPU launches for every token to replay.
concepts.why: A warm compile cache cut compiling to 0.33 s; graph capture took the same time in every arm, cached or not.

results.read_as: The coloured segments are most of the wait, and where the two caches act. Platform time is a residual found by subtraction, not just queueing. Medians do not add: these sum to 82.49 s, not the 81.12 s median total.

recall.q: Why does KV cache size limit concurrency, and what changes if requests get shorter?
recall.a: Each request keeps K and V for every token so far, so its cache grows with its length. The cache is a token budget: shorter requests fit more of them.

recall.q: Why must the engine run the model once before serving anyone?
recall.a: Free memory depends on what a forward pass needs, and the only way to know is to run one at the largest batch, record the peak, and give the rest to the KV cache.

recall.q: Why can a cold compile cost KV cache capacity, not only seconds?
recall.a: The compiler's working memory is still on the GPU during profiling, so the profiler sees less free memory and sizes a smaller cache for the replica's whole life.

recall.q: What do you trade by skipping CUDA graph capture?
recall.a: Capture removes per-step launch overhead from every later token. Skipping it saves startup once and pays on every token: arguably fine for a short-lived replica only.

recall.q: Why is a compile cache more fragile than a weight cache?
recall.a: Its key includes engine version, model, GPU and flags, which change routinely, so an upgrade silently makes it cold. Weights never change.

recall.q: What changes if a new replica lands on a host that never pulled the image?
recall.a: The image pull happens before your code runs, and neither cache touches it: artifact 1's one such run took 2266.6 s.
